subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp. 89–92): read the informational text aloud together.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the opening paragraph aloud, pausing to unpack the word 'Hekko' — 'Hek' means challenge, 'ko' means tiger. Students listen with books open at pp. 89–90.

Teacher reads the folk story of Aami and Aakho aloud, modelling expression; students follow in their texts. Pause at each new word — declared, superiority, disagreement, surrender — and invite a quick show of hands on guessed meanings.
Shared reading of pp. 91–92 describing the modern game: teacher reads a sentence, students echo-read the same sentence. Draw attention to how the game rules are laid out as steps.
Let us Read (pp. 89–92): brief whole-class oral recap — teacher asks 'Who are the two teams?' and 'What is the circle used for?' as a comprehension check. Students answer in one sentence each.

periods.teacher_notes: The chapter's Naga vocabulary — Hekko, Aami, Aakho, Joko, Khozuba, Khotiba — is central to meaning; write each term on the board as it appears. The folk-story origin of the game gives purpose to the rules that follow, so read it unhurriedly before moving to the game description.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for key Naga terms

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion — Let us Think A

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 93): answer five questions about Hekko in writing.

homework.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 93): write two sentences about which team you would choose and why.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the rules section of the text (pp. 91–92) aloud once more while students follow. This brief re-encounter refreshes the game details before discussion begins.

Let us Think A (p. 93): teacher reads questions 1–3 aloud; students think-pair-share answers before writing. Circulate to check that 'Hekko = challenging the tiger' and the team names Aami and Aakho are stated accurately.

Let us Think A (p. 93): teacher reads questions 4 and 5 aloud; students discuss in pairs then write individually. For question 5 — why Aakho must say 'Joko' — prompt students to connect surrender in the game with the folk story's resolution.
Whole-class share-out of written answers; teacher selects two or three responses per question to read aloud and gives brief oral feedback on accuracy and sentence form.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 5 is inferential — students may need a nudge to link 'Joko' (surrender) back to the folk story's theme of accepting defeat gracefully. Accept varied personal reasoning as long as it is grounded in the text.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p. 98): listen to five game descriptions and name each game.

time_bands.activity: Brief warm-up: teacher asks students to name any traditional game from their own state or neighbourhood. Take three or four responses to activate prior knowledge before the listening begins.
Let us Listen (p. 98): teacher reads the transcript for all five game descriptions aloud at a natural pace (first reading). Students listen with pencils down; no writing yet.
Teacher reads the transcript a second time, pausing after each description. Students jot a game name in their exercise books. A third reading allows them to confirm or revise.

Whole-class oral share-out: teacher invites one student per description to say the game name aloud and give one reason for their answer. Confirm correct responses — Pitthu/Lagori, Kabaddi, Gilli-Danda, Antakshari arch game, Marbles.

periods.teacher_notes: Read each description at an unhurried pace and avoid pausing mid-sentence; the clues are cumulative within each description. If students are uncertain about game names, accept descriptive answers and supply the conventional name after discussion.

periods.activity_title: Speaking — Games I Know and Love

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak A (p. 100): look at pictures, identify games, discuss favourites with a partner.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or refers students to the six illustrations on p. 100. Class does a quick picture walk — teacher points to each image and students call out what they see the children doing.

Let us Speak A (p. 100): in pairs, students discuss which games they recognise and whether they have played any. Teacher circulates, listening and prompting with 'What do you like about that game?' and 'How is it played?' to extend responses beyond one-word answers.

Each pair selects their favourite game from the pictures and prepares a two-sentence statement: the game's name and one reason they enjoy it. Partners practise saying it aloud to each other before the share-out.
Four or five pairs share their favourite game and reason with the class. Teacher notes any game named that connects to the Hekko chapter theme of traditional Indian sports.

periods.teacher_notes: The six pictures on p. 100 show games students may know by different regional names; accept all regional names and write the common name alongside. Encourage students to speak in full sentences rather than single words.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p. 94): choose the correct homophone to complete each sentence.
Let us Learn B (p. 95): look at pictures and write names using 'st', 'ch', 'gl' blends.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five homophone pairs on the board — their/there, two/too, through/threw, caught/cot, right/write — and reads each pair aloud. Students repeat chorally; teacher clarifies meaning differences with a quick example sentence for each.

Let us Learn A (p. 94–95): teacher reads each sentence frame aloud with a deliberate pause at the blank. Students select the correct homophone by raising hands; teacher then asks the class to write the answer in their books. Work through all ten sentences together.

Let us Learn B (p. 95): teacher introduces the three blends — 'st', 'ch', 'gl' — with a quick blend-and-say drill (stairs, chain, gloves). Students then look at the nine pictures and write the name of each item independently.
Pair-check: students compare their blend word answers with a partner. Whole class reads all nine words aloud together; teacher corrects any mis-spelled blend at the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The homophones 'through/threw' and 'caught/cot' cause the most confusion at this stage — write both words in a sample sentence on the board so students see the contrast in context. For consonant blends, insist on blending both letters before the vowel rather than sounding letters separately.
materials: Blackboard for homophone pairs and blend drill

periods.activity_title: Animal Sounds, Past Tense, and -ed Verbs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (p. 96): match six animals to their sounds.
Let us Learn E (p. 97): fill in ten blanks with the -ed past-tense form.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn C (p. 96): teacher reads each animal name aloud — Tiger, Horse, Elephant, Dove, Goat, Monkey — and students try to produce the sound word before the teacher supplies it. Students then draw lines in their books to match animal to sound.

Teacher reads the three example sentences from Let us Learn D (p. 96) aloud — 'lived', 'declared', 'challenged' — and writes them on the board. Elicit the rule: add -ed to most verbs for past tense; introduce three irregular forms (came, drank, saw) with brief example sentences. This is a teacher-led discussion, not a separate written task.

Let us Learn E (p. 97): teacher reads the passage aloud once while students follow. Students then fill in all ten blanks independently, applying the -ed rule. Circulate and note any irregular-verb slips.
Quick oral correction: teacher reads each sentence and cold-calls students to supply the -ed form. Write any error on the board and correct it together.

periods.teacher_notes: Let us Learn D is used here as a teacher-led bridge to Let us Learn E rather than as a separate written exercise — this keeps the grammar in context and within available time. The passage in Let us Learn E features a park visit and a game of kabaddi, which connects naturally to the chapter's theme of traditional sports.
materials: Blackboard for -ed examples and irregular verbs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p. 101): write about a new game using the given format.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the Hekko game structure — two teams, a circle, specific roles, points, special titles — and writes the six format headings on the board: Game name, Time, Number of players, Material needed, Rules, Foul. Students read the headings aloud together.

Teacher models a brief example game using the six headings ('Cloud Tag': two teams, ten minutes, no equipment, etc.) by filling each heading on the board in one or two sentences. Think aloud about decisions: 'How many players makes it fair? What counts as a foul?'

Let us Write A (p. 101): students plan and draft their own new game using the six headings independently in their exercise books. Teacher circulates and gives one-sentence written or oral feedback on clarity of rules.
Three or four students share their game name and one rule aloud. Class gives a quick thumbs-up if the rule is clear. Students make any final corrections to their draft.

periods.teacher_notes: The six-heading format on p. 101 scaffolds the writing task so students focus on content rather than organisation. Encourage students to keep rules short and specific — one action per rule sentence — so the game is easy to understand from the written description.
materials: Blackboard for format headings and model

periods.activity_title: Exploring the Hornbill Festival of Nagaland

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore (p. 101): find out about the Hornbill festival and share findings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the Hekko game to its cultural home: Nagaland is known for its festivals as well as its traditional sports. Ask students what they already know about Nagaland or its festivals — take brief responses and write any Hornbill details mentioned on the board.

Let us Explore (p. 101): in groups of three or four, students discuss and pool what they know or can reason about the Hornbill festival — when it might be held, what it might celebrate, what activities could feature. Each group appoints a note-keeper who jots two or three facts.

Each group shares their two or three points with the class. Teacher supplements with key facts: Hornbill is held in December, celebrates Naga tribal culture through dance, music, food, and traditional games including sports like Hekko. Students add any new information to their notes.

Each student writes two sentences in their exercise book: one fact about the Hornbill festival and one sentence connecting it to the chapter's theme of traditional sports and cultural heritage. Two or three students read their sentences aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about Hekko as a game rooted in Naga folk tradition, students are well placed to appreciate the Hornbill festival as a broader cultural celebration from the same region. Encourage students to name specific elements — music, dance, food, games — rather than giving a vague 'it is a festival of Nagaland' response.

items.item_stem: In the game of Hekko, what must an Aakho player say when caught by the Aami team, and what happens after they say it?

options.label: A
options.text: They say 'Aami', and they are allowed to switch teams for the rest of the game.

options.label: B
options.text: They say 'Hekko', and the game is immediately paused while the referee counts points.

options.label: C
options.text: They say 'Joko', which means surrender, and are then released so another Aakho player can enter the circle.

options.label: D
options.text: They say 'Khozuba', and they are given the title of fastest player on the Aakho side.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have confused the game name 'Hekko' with the surrender call, or not read the rules carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has mixed up the special title 'Khozuba' (fastest Aami player) with the surrender protocol.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may not have understood the team roles are fixed and that 'Aami' is a team name, not a call.

items.source_lo: Student reads and retrieves information using an informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Hekko game: origin folk story, Aami and Aakho teams, rules, scoring, special titles.
items.item_stem: The chapter explains that Hekko began as a disagreement between Aami (humans) and Aakho (tigers) about who was superior. In the modern game, what do the Aami players do inside the circle, and how does the game end? Write two to three sentences using details from the text.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The Aami players stay inside the circle and form a human chain to protect themselves from being pushed out. Two Aakho players enter at a time and try to push Aami players out of the circle. The game ends when all Aakho players are caught, all Aami players are pushed out, or time runs out — the team with the most points wins.

items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the description below aloud. Listen carefully and decide whether the statement that follows is true or false.

Description: In this game, one player from a team crosses into the other team's side. While there, the player must keep chanting the name of the game without stopping to take a breath. The player tries to tag as many opponents as possible and return safely to their own side. If the player is caught before returning, the opposing team scores a point.

Statement: In this game, the player who crosses to the other side must chant the name of the game without stopping.

options.text: In this game, the player who crosses to the other side must chant the name of the game without stopping.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: True. The description states that the player must keep chanting the name of the game continuously without taking a breath while on the opposing team's side.

items.item_stem:
Read the sentence below and fill in the blank to make it a complete rule for a new game.

In my new game, a player is out if they ________________________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Answers will vary; accept any logical rule completion that describes a clear action resulting in a player being eliminated (e.g. 'step outside the marked boundary' or 'drop the ball before reaching the goal line').

items.item_stem: Just as the people of Nagaland created Hekko with its own name, teams, and rules, invent a new game of your own. Use the headings below to write about it: Game name / Number of players / One rule / One foul.

expected_elements: Game name and player count clearly stated.
Rule is specific and describes one player action.
Foul describes a prohibited action with a consequence.

items.source_context: Simple past tense: adding -ed to regular verbs; illustrated through a park-visit passage.
items.item_stem: Read each sentence. Decide whether the underlined verb is in the correct past-tense form. Write TRUE if it is correct, or FALSE if it is not.

options.text: He enjoyed watching the traditional game with his friends.
Last week, she jointed her teammates on the field before the game started.
The referee pointed to the boundary line and the team stoped running.
Yesterday, the children played kabaddi in the park for an hour.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — 'played' is the correct -ed form of 'play'.  2. False — the correct form is 'joined', not 'jointed'.  3. False — 'pointed' is correct but 'stoped' should be 'stopped' (double the final consonant before -ed).  4. True — 'enjoyed' is the correct -ed form of 'enjoy'.
